item.title: pbakaus/impeccable
item.description:
The design vocabulary for your coding agent. Steer with polish and bolder, review with critique and audit, catch AI slop before it ships.

https://impeccable.style

Impeccable

The design vocabulary for your coding agent. Steer with polish and bolder, review with critique and audit, and catch AI slop before it ships.

From your project root:

npx impeccable install

Reload your coding tool, then run /impeccable init in your agent ($impeccable init on Codex).

Works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot, Devin, Replit Agent, Gemini CLI, Grok Build, OpenCode, Google Antigravity, Kiro, Trae, Rovo Dev, Qoder, Mistral Vibe, Pi, Hermes Agent, DeepSeek Harness, and Veto. Full docs live at impeccable.style/docs.

Without Impeccable With Impeccable

Same model (Fable 5.1), same brief: a fourteen-room family guesthouse on the Ligurian coast. Without Impeccable, it builds the tasteful default: cream page, thin serif, italic accent, pill buttons. With it, the page is built around one picture: the house at night, seen from the water.

For a full project, see the Neo Mirai case study: a conference site taken from mockup to shipped page.

Why

Inter for everything. Purple-to-blue gradients. Cards nested in cards, gray text on colored backgrounds, a rounded-square icon tile above every heading. Ask an agent for a page with no other guidance and these show up again and again, across models and projects.

  • Words for what you want. "Make it pop" leaves your agent to guess. /impeccable bolder the pricing cards loads a playbook written for that one move and points it at one target.
  • A reviewer. critique scores the design against usability heuristics and ranks what to fix first. audit checks accessibility, performance, theming, and responsive behavior, with findings ranked P0 (blocking) to P3 (polish).
  • A slop detector. 62 deterministic rules flag the tells above, plus quality problems like cramped padding and skipped headings. No LLM, no API key.

Impeccable is strongest on interfaces that already exist: point it at a page or a component and iterate. It builds new pages too; see Build something new for how to get the most out of that harder mode. To start, pick one component:

/impeccable critique the pricing cards

How it works

Run /impeccable init once per project. It reads your code, asks only what it can't infer (who the product is for, what it needs to do, the constraints), and writes PRODUCT.md. Every later command reads it. Run /impeccable document to capture your existing visual system in DESIGN.md, so changes stay on-brand. More on context files.

Then name a command and a target:

/impeccable critique the onboarding flow
/impeccable quieter the landing page
/impeccable polish settings
/impeccable harden checkout

Or just describe what you want: /impeccable redo this hero section. Narrow targets get better results; a single section reviewed closely beats a whole page at a glance. Pin a command you use often with /impeccable pin audit to get /audit as its own shortcut.

24 commands

Commands
Steer bolder amplifies safe designs · quieter tones down loud ones · distill removes what the page doesn't need · colorize brings color to a gray interface · typeset fixes fonts, hierarchy, and sizing · layout fixes spacing and rhythm · animate adds transitions and interaction feedback · delight adds personality · overdrive goes for shaders, spring physics, and scroll-driven effects
Review critique is a scored UX review · audit is a technical quality report
Finish polish is the final pass before shipping · harden covers errors, i18n, overflow, and edge cases · clarify rewrites unclear copy · adapt handles screen sizes and devices · optimize fixes loading and rendering performance · onboard designs first-run flows and empty states
Iterate live live lets you pick an element in the browser and cycle through variants · generate produces variants of a named element without manual picking
Plan and set up shape plans UX before code · init writes PRODUCT.md · document writes DESIGN.md · extract pulls repeated patterns into your design system

The 24th, craft, is a deprecated alias for a plain build request. Type /impeccable alone to see the list in your agent. Each command has its own page: impeccable.style/docs.

On Codex, open /skills or type $impeccable instead of the slash command.

Live mode

/impeccable live opens your running dev server with an overlay. Select an element, pick a direction, and Impeccable hot-swaps variants in place. Accept one and it is written back to your source. It works with Vite, Next, SvelteKit, Astro, Nuxt, and plain HTML. Iterate in the browser.

Live mode edits a local checkout only; don't inject it into a deployed site or weaken a production CSP to make it work. Applying copy edits runs your package.json's optional impeccable:manual-edit-validate script with your permissions, so review it before using live mode in an unfamiliar repo.

Apply sends staged copy edits to your chat agent while a live session is polling. If none has polled in the last minute, it runs the codex CLI from your PATH instead (or claude when codex is missing), with approvals, permission checks, and sandboxing off (--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox or --permission-mode bypassPermissions) and your environment inherited. Its prompt carries the staged edits, the edited elements' HTML and nearby text, the page URL, and candidate source paths. Set IMPECCABLE_LIVE_COPY_AGENT=chat in the environment that starts live mode to keep Apply in your chat session, or off to disable Apply. The server reads it once at startup.

Three ways to run the detector

In your agent. The design hook scans every UI file your agent edits and hands the findings back before the agent calls the work done. This is where most slop gets caught: without the hook, the detector only runs when someone remembers to run it. It's available on Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Grok Build, and Hermes Agent, and the installer sets it up. Say yes. Automatic design checks.

In CI or your terminal. The CLI needs no agent:

npx impeccable detect src/                   # scan a directory
npx impeccable detect https://example.com    # scan a rendered page (uses your installed Chrome or Edge)
npx impeccable detect --json .               # machine-readable output
npx impeccable detect --github src/          # GitHub Actions annotations
npx impeccable detect --list-rules           # every rule with its id and description

Source files like JSX and TSX get the pattern rules only. Rules that need a rendered page, such as low contrast and tiny text, run when you scan a URL, so point the CLI at your dev server too: npx impeccable detect http://localhost:5173.

Exit code 2 means findings, 1 means a target couldn't be scanned. To allow your brand font everywhere, run npx impeccable ignores add-value overused-font Inter --reason "Brand font". To turn a rule off for one file, add a comment: <!-- impeccable-disable overused-font: exported brand doc -->. Run a detector scan · Configuration and ignores.

In your browser. The Chrome extension overlays the same findings on any live page, yours or anyone else's. Review with a visual overlay.

Installation

npx impeccable install

The installer detects your coding tools, asks whether to install for this project or globally, and offers the design hook where your tool supports one. Accept the hook. Reload your tool afterward. npx impeccable update refreshes an existing install. For scripts, pass --providers=claude,codex,cursor and --scope=project|global.

Three tools need one more step before the hook runs. In Codex, open /hooks and approve the project hook (again after an update that changes it). In Grok Build, run /hooks-trust or launch with --trust. In Hermes Agent, the hook is a plugin: run hermes plugins enable impeccable-design-hook once. Allow the hook in your harness.

Node is only needed for npx. The skill itself runs a self-contained engine binary that ships next to it or downloads once into ~/.impeccable/bin/.

Claude Code, Copilot, and Grok plugins

Claude Code: /plugin marketplace add pbakaus/impeccable, then open /plugin and install Impeccable.

GitHub Copilot in VS Code: install Impeccable from the Visual Studio Marketplace or run code --install-extension renaissance-geek.impeccable. Needs VS Code 1.109.3+, Copilot Chat, and a trusted workspace. It installs the skill without the hook. Details.

Grok Build: grok plugin install pbakaus/impeccable#plugin --trust installs the skill, agents, and hook.

Git submodule (a pinned version for the whole team) 
git submodule add https://github.com/pbakaus/impeccable vendor/impeccable
npx impeccable link --source=vendor/impeccable --providers=claude,cursor

Commit .gitmodules, the submodule, and the generated links. Teammates run git submodule update --init --recursive. To upgrade, run git submodule update --remote vendor/impeccable, rerun the link command, and commit. Linking installs skills, not hooks. Existing skill folders stay put unless you pass --force.

Manual copy, no Node required

Download the ZIP for your tool from impeccable.style, or clone this repo: each tool's build is committed at the repo root. Copy skills/impeccable from the folder below into the same place in your project, or into the global folder.

Tool Repo folder Global skills folder
Claude Code .claude/ ~/.claude/skills/
Cursor .cursor/
Codex CLI, Replit Agent .agents/ ~/.agents/skills/
Devin .devin/ ${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/devin/skills/
GitHub Copilot .github/
Gemini CLI .gemini/
Google Antigravity .agent/ ~/.gemini/config/skills/
OpenCode .opencode/
Grok Build .grok/ ~/.grok/skills/
Hermes Agent .hermes/ ${HERMES_HOME:-$HOME/.hermes}/skills/
DeepSeek Harness .dsh/ ${DSH_HOME:-$HOME/.dsh}/skills/
Pi .pi/
Qoder .qoder/ ~/.qoder/skills/
Rovo Dev .rovodev/ ~/.rovodev/skills/
Mistral Vibe .vibe/ ~/.vibe/skills/
Trae .trae/ ~/.trae/skills/
Trae China .trae-cn/ ~/.trae-cn/skills/

For example: mkdir -p your-project/.claude/skills && cp -r .claude/skills/impeccable your-project/.claude/skills/.

Notes:

  • A manual copy skips the design hook and subagents. Run npx impeccable install to get them; it writes each tool's hook pointing at the right skill path.
  • OpenCode also needs .opencode/commands/impeccable.md copied into your project's .opencode/commands/ to provide /impeccable.
  • Hermes asks you to trust project-local skills once: run hermes skills trust from the project root. Global installs need no trust step.
  • Cursor and Gemini CLI may need Agent Skills enabled in settings. See the Cursor and Gemini CLI skills docs.
  • Restart Trae after copying.
  • impeccable install and update manage a DeepSeek Harness global copy only when DSH_HOME is inside your home directory.

Project files and git

Impeccable writes its working files under .impeccable/. A few are shared project artifacts and belong in the repo: config.json, live/config.json, design.json, surfaces/*.md, and critique/*.md. Keep PRODUCT.md and DESIGN.md in the repo too. The rest is screenshots, caches, and runtime state.

Copy the .gitignore entries 
# impeccable-ignore-start
# Ephemeral output, runtime state, and per-dev overrides.
# The **/ prefix covers .impeccable at the repo root or in a nested workspace.
# Shared artifacts stay tracked: config.json, live/config.json,
# design.json, surfaces/*.md, critique/*.md.
**/.impeccable/config.local.json
**/.impeccable/hook.cache.json
**/.impeccable/hook.pending.json
**/.impeccable/*.png
**/.impeccable/review/
**/.impeccable/questions/
**/.impeccable/live/server.json
**/.impeccable/live/sessions/
**/.impeccable/live/previews/
**/.impeccable/live/annotations/
**/.impeccable/live/cache/
**/.impeccable/live/manual-edit-apply-transaction.json
**/.impeccable/live/manual-edit-events.jsonl
**/.impeccable/live/manual-edit-evidence/
**/.impeccable/live/pending-manual-edits.json
**/.impeccable/live/deferred-svelte-component-accepts.json
**/.impeccable/live/*.png
# impeccable-ignore-end

The folders that hold decision-round state (.impeccable/questions/, .impeccable/mocks/worlds/) also ignore themselves. A .gitignore can't untrack a file git already tracks; if you committed one earlier, run git rm --cached <path>.

Good to know

Build path. For new landing pages and showcase surfaces, Impeccable can generate a full-fidelity comp first and build to match it (bolder, slower), or build straight in code (leaner, faster). App screens and documents are always built in code. init asks once and saves the answer as buildPath in .impeccable/config.json; the decision page lets you override it for one session. The choice only appears when your harness can generate images. Image generation · Configuration.

Native apps. Set ## Platform in PRODUCT.md to ios, android, or adaptive (one Flutter or React Native codebase that follows each OS), and the design commands work from Apple's HIG or Material 3 instead of web conventions. init asks when it can't tell. audit and adapt switch to native versions, and the native audit reads SwiftUI, Compose, React Native, or Flutter source directly. The detector, live mode with its generate shortcut, and the edit hook stay web-only, because they work on HTML and CSS in a browser.

Hooks run outside model approval. In Claude Code, installed command hooks run even when you deny the model's own commands, so the first edit can download the engine. Review installed hooks before unattended runs, or pass --settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}' to turn them off for a run. The installer leaves hook entries it didn't add alone.

Something broken? /impeccable doctor finds stale context files, unused settings, and broken hooks. Fix setup problems.

Telemetry. When a new design starts, the skill fetches a set of visual directions from the impeccable.style catalog. Turning telemetry off doesn't stop that request; it stops the anonymous record of which directions were shown and which one you picked, which is how the catalog learns what works. Your project name, files, code, and PRODUCT.md are never sent. Disable telemetry with npx impeccable telemetry off, DO_NOT_TRACK=1, or "telemetry": false in .impeccable/config.json for the whole project. The full list of what is sent is on the privacy page.

Community

  • Issues for bugs, questions, and ideas. Outside contributions start with an issue; see DEVELOP.md.
  • Changelog for what shipped.
  • Follow @pbakaus for release notes and new rules.

Sponsors

Thanks to Namespace for sponsoring Impeccable's CI with fast Linux and Windows runners.

License

Apache 2.0. See LICENSE. Impeccable started from Anthropic's frontend-design skill.

item.title: vercel-labs/agent-browser
item.description:
Browser automation CLI for AI agents

https://agent-browser.dev

agent-browser

Browser automation for AI agents: open pages, read them as an accessibility tree, and act on elements from the shell.

agent-browser is a native Rust CLI that gives an AI agent a browser it can drive one command at a time. snapshot returns the page as compact text with a ref such as @e1 for each element. The agent acts on a ref, reads the page again to check the result, and repeats. The browser stays open between commands, so each step is one short shell call.

Install

npm install -g agent-browser
agent-browser install           # download Chrome for Testing (first time only)
  • Homebrew: brew install agent-browser, then agent-browser install.
  • Linux: agent-browser install --with-deps also installs the browser's system libraries.
  • No install: npx agent-browser open example.com.

Project installs, building from source, upgrade, and doctor are covered in Installation.

Quick start

agent-browser open example.com
agent-browser snapshot -i       # interactive elements, each with a ref
agent-browser click @e1         # act on a ref from that snapshot
agent-browser get url           # check the result
agent-browser close

The snapshot for example.com:

- link "Learn more" [ref=e1]
  • Refs describe the page at the time of the snapshot. After navigation or a DOM change, take a new snapshot before using refs again.
  • CSS selectors, text, XPath, and semantic locators also work, for example agent-browser find role button click --name "Submit". See Selectors.
  • A click fails, instead of reporting success, when the target is hidden, disabled, outside the viewport, or covered by another element such as a consent banner. Dismiss the covering element, take a new snapshot, and retry.

The full walkthrough is in the quick start.

How it works

The CLI sends each command to a background daemon that starts on the first command and controls the browser over the Chrome DevTools Protocol. Each --session gets its own daemon and browser. By default, the daemon closes a headless browser and exits after one hour without commands, saving state first when session persistence is configured.

Chrome for Testing is the default browser. You can also attach to a running Chrome with --cdp or --auto-connect (CDP mode), select the Lightpanda or Obscura engine with --engine, drive Mobile Safari in the iOS Simulator, or use a cloud browser provider such as Browserbase, Browserless, Browser Use, Kernel, or AgentCore.

For AI agents

The CLI ships skills that match its version:

agent-browser skills get core                 # the core loop, refs, waiting, and common workflows
agent-browser skills get core --ref commands  # one reference, such as the full command list
agent-browser skills get core --full          # adds the full command reference and templates
agent-browser skills list                     # specialized skills: electron, slack, dogfood, and more

Install the discovery skill into an agent harness from skills.sh:

npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-browser

The installed skill is a thin stub that tells the agent to load agent-browser skills get core, so its instructions always match the installed CLI. Or add this to your AGENTS.md:

Use `agent-browser` for browser automation. Before the first use, run
`agent-browser skills get core` and follow it.

For MCP clients, agent-browser mcp starts an MCP server over stdio. See MCP server.

Commands

Run agent-browser --help for the full list, or agent-browser <command> --help for one command.

Group Commands Docs
Navigate and read open, back, forward, reload, read, snapshot, get, is Core, Snapshots
Interact click, dblclick, fill, type, press, keyboard, hover, focus, select, check, uncheck, scroll, drag, upload, mouse, find Core, Find elements
Wait wait Wait
Capture screenshot, pdf, record, download, diff Recording, Diffing, Files
Page and network state cookies, storage, network, set, clipboard, eval, pushstate Network, Settings
Tabs, frames, and dialogs tab, frame, dialog Tabs and frames
Debug and performance console, errors, highlight, inspect, trace, profiler, vitals, react, a11y Debugging, Profiler, React
Sessions and auth session, state, auth, profiles, confirm, deny Sessions, Security
Agents and integrations skills, mcp, webmcp, flow, chat, batch, plugin Skills, WebMCP, Plugins
Observe stream, dashboard Streaming, Dashboard
Setup install, upgrade, doctor, connect, close Installation

Flags, environment variables, and agent-browser.json are documented in Configuration.

Platforms

Native binaries ship for macOS (ARM64, x64), Linux (ARM64, x64, glibc and musl), and Windows (x64). The npm package picks the right binary for the host.

Development

Building from source requires Node.js 24 or later, pnpm 11 or later, and Rust:

pnpm install
pnpm build:source               # builds the dashboard and the native CLI
pnpm link --global
agent-browser install

Run the Rust checks from cli/:

cargo fmt -- --check
cargo clippy
cargo test
cargo test e2e -- --ignored --test-threads=1   # launches real headless Chrome

AGENTS.md lists the files to update with each change, the docs checks, and the release process.

Documentation

  • agent-browser.dev: introduction, guides, and reference
  • Commands and Configuration
  • Security: the auth vault, domain allowlists, action policies, and content boundaries
  • Next.js and Vercel and eve: running agent-browser in Vercel Sandbox and eve agents
  • Changelog

License

Apache-2.0

item.title: akitaonrails/ai-memory
item.description:
Solution for long term memory for agent coding CLIs and to facilitate handoff between different agent vendors

Long-term memory for AI coding agents. Quit Claude Code mid-task, start OpenAI Codex in the same directory, continue without re-explaining the architecture, the failed approaches, or the open questions.

Website: aimemory.sh

Why ai-memory

Your coding agent probably has a memory feature already. Claude Code takes its own notes, Cursor remembers some things, and every platform is adding more. They all have the same limits: the notes live on one machine, belong to one agent, and drop out of view when you switch tools or hand the work to a teammate.

ai-memory removes those limits.

  • It follows you across agents. More than twenty harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Grok, Devin, Kimi, Kiro, and others) feed one shared memory. Quit Claude Code mid-task, open Codex in the same directory, and the next agent picks up a handoff that says where you left off, what failed, and what is still open. Handoffs are a typed protocol: each one has an owner and is claimed exactly once.

  • It can carry the session, not just a summary. Start agents with ai-memory run: quit Claude Code, run ai-memory run codex, and Codex gets the shared workstream plus a private, temporary local projection of Claude's visible native history for exact details the bounded startup packet omitted. The remote server receives only the harness and session identity, never the local transcript path or body. Direct harness launches behave exactly as before.

  • It follows you across projects. A small profile of how you usually work (your package manager, test layout, architecture habits) reaches every new repository at session start, so you stop re-explaining yourself. It sits below each repository's rules file as a default. It is on by default for a single user, and on a shared server it is opt-in and private per person. See docs/cross-project-profile.md.

  • It follows you across machines. Memory lives in a server you run, on the same laptop, a homelab box, or anywhere else, so the project you left on the desktop is the project you resume on the laptop, with the same knowledge and the same open questions.

  • It works for a team. Point everyone at one server, and what one person's sessions learn, everyone's agents can retrieve. Knowledge is shared per project; personal handoffs stay personal. Multi-user auth, per-person attribution, and an audit log are built in and are not a paid tier.

  • Your memory is plain markdown. The source of truth is a git-backed wiki of ordinary .md files: grep it, open it in Obsidian, edit it by hand, rsync it. The database is a derived index that can always be rebuilt from the files. There is no vector store to maintain and no content locked in a binary blob.

  • It captures the work itself, silently. Lifecycle hooks record what happened (prompts, tool calls, session boundaries), sanitize it at a typed privacy boundary before anything is stored, and the server consolidates it into readable pages. You do not have to ask it to remember anything. The default path uses zero LLM calls: capture, search, and handoffs all work with no API key.

  • It ages memory without an LLM. Memory decays on a schedule you can tune per tier, and memory you use decays slower: opening a page, searching it, or reaching it through a link counts as use. When episodic notes go cold they can be compacted down to their durable facts (file paths, error codes, decisions) instead of dropped. Near-duplicates collapse into one, and likely contradictions get flagged, all with zero API calls. Nothing is hard-deleted: the original stays in git and the version chain (restore-page brings it back). Access-weighted retention is always on because it can only keep memory longer. The parts that rewrite or drop content (compaction, dedup, per-tier curves) stay off by default until you turn them on.

  • It can also "dream", if you let it. With an LLM configured, an opt-in background pass rewrites whole clusters of cold notes into single coherent pages while you are idle, and cancels as soon as you come back to work. It never deletes a source (the pre-merge versions stay reachable), it is off by default, and it has to pass a recall eval before it could become default behavior. Unless you ask for more, the zero-LLM path above is what runs.

  • It is honest about itself. It ships as one self-contained binary. Purge commands say exactly what "deleted" means. The write ceiling (~700/s) is measured, not guessed. An audit log records every mutation.

How it works

capture ──▶ consolidate ──▶ recall ──▶ handoff
 hooks        session-end      search     next agent,
 observe      summaries as     + brief    any harness
 silently     wiki pages       injection

Agents emit sanitized observations through lifecycle hooks as you work. At session end, observations become coherent markdown pages in the project's wiki (optionally LLM-written; useful even without). The next session, in any agent on any machine, gets a bounded brief and can search everything: full-text, entities, links, and (optionally) vectors, fused into one ranking. Cross-agent handoffs pass the baton explicitly.

The full design, including the invariants that keep multi-user and multi-session use safe, is in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md.

An optional server-rendered management console provides user administration, session inspection and deletion, and personal MCP API keys. Build with --features management-ui and start serve --transport http --enable-management-ui; both compile-time and runtime opt-ins are required.

Support matrix

Every row below is a first-party integration (MCP registration, lifecycle hooks, or both) checked by CI. The full matrix with per-agent notes and caveats is in docs/support-matrix.md.

Coming from another tool?

Most agent-memory tools optimize for one thing: extracting atomic facts per turn, a temporal knowledge graph, an agent-editable memory OS, or a hosted context API. ai-memory is built around a git-backed markdown wiki as the source of truth, with a derived index for retrieval. It captures automatically from lifecycle hooks, is shared across agents, machines, and people, and works with zero LLM calls by default. This table shows what carries over from each tool and what you gain:

Coming from… What's similar What you gain
Mem0 / fact extractors (LangMem) Automatic per-turn capture Memory compiles into readable pages you own and edit, not opaque fact rows; retrieval fuses FTS + entity + graph (+ local vectors) with no cloud API key
Zep / Graphiti (temporal KG) Temporal reasoning, typed relations Bi-temporal-lite (as_of, version-filtered search) and typed edges without standing up a graph database, in one binary
mcp-memory-service (fact rows, SQLite) SQLite + local embeddings, hook capture, typed edges, honest numbers, and, on 2.4, per-tier decay curves, extractive compression, DBSCAN cold-cluster dedup, access reinforcement, and contradiction flagging Human-editable markdown pages instead of fact-rows, cross-agent claim-once handoffs, and the same aging machinery done zero-LLM by default, reversibly (supersede-not-delete + restore-page), and off by default
basic-memory (file-first markdown) Markdown-on-disk as the source of truth Automatic lifecycle capture and a derived FTS/entity/graph index on top, cross-agent handoffs, and multi-user sharing built in
Claude Code built-in memory "Remember my project" convenience, zero setup Synced across machines and agents, searchable, team-capable, and captures tool lifecycle, unlike a per-laptop MEMORY.md
Hindsight / OpenViking (LLM or VLM in the loop) Living pages / document memory with a background consolidation loop, plus, on 2.4, belief-strength confidence plus an opt-in LLM "dream" rewrite of cold clusters A self-contained binary that runs zero-LLM by default and keeps memory in markdown files that are the source of truth, not a mirror; claim-once handoffs; the dream/belief features are opt-in, off by default, and never delete a source (vs a mandatory LLM loop)
Supermemory / LiquidLM (hosted memory API) A managed second brain with automatic ingestion Git-versioned markdown you own, no required API spend, offline operation, and per-project team sharing; ai-memory remembers this repo, not a general vault

Across all of these, ai-memory gives you files you own (git-backed markdown), a zero-LLM default, one self-contained binary, sharing across agents, machines, and teams, automatic lifecycle capture, and typed, claim-once handoffs. Opt-in features (LLM consolidation, vector search, the "dream" consolidation pass, belief-strength in ranking) stay opt-in, and the zero-LLM aging path (per-tier decay, extractive compaction, dedup, contradiction flagging, access-weighted retention) works with no API key at all.

Built on the shoulders of: the Karpathy LLM Wiki (compile-not-retrieve), agentmemory (hook capture for coding agents), basic-memory (markdown-on-disk truth), cognee (pipeline composition and triplet embeddings), Hermes Agent (the self-improvement loop), and A-MEM (Zettelkasten-style atomic notes).

The full comparison, covering where each approach wins, where ai-memory differs, and the published benchmark, is in How ai-memory compares.

Quick start

Linux and macOS (two commands, no root)

curl -fsSL https://github.com/akitaonrails/ai-memory/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
ai-memory setup

install.sh downloads the release for your OS and CPU, checks it against the release's published SHA-256 checksum (it refuses to install without a match), and links ~/.local/bin/ai-memory. ai-memory setup then creates the data directory with a bearer token in an owner-only file, starts a per-user service (systemd --user or a launchd LaunchAgent), and wires MCP, hooks and Agent Skills for every agent it finds, or the ones you name with --agent. It shows the plan, with where it found each agent, and asks first: answer y, or type the numbers of the agents to wire. --plan prints the plan and changes nothing, --web shows the plan as a page in your browser and applies the agents you tick there, --yes skips the question, and running it again changes nothing. Afterwards, restart your agents and ask one of them "What do you remember about this project?" to see it answer through ai-memory. Details, the environment variables and how to verify the script before running it are in docs/install.md. An AI agent installing ai-memory for you can follow INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md.

Claude Code and Codex users can wire their agent as a marketplace plugin instead (the binary is still installed as above):

claude plugin marketplace add akitaonrails/ai-memory && claude plugin install ai-memory@ai-memory
codex plugin marketplace add akitaonrails/ai-memory && codex plugin add ai-memory@ai-memory

Codex then asks you to trust the hooks in /hooks. See Marketplace plugins.

Windows (two commands, no admin)

In PowerShell:

irm https://github.com/akitaonrails/ai-memory/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex
ai-memory setup

install.ps1 checks the release zip against its published SHA-256 checksum, unpacks it under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\ai-memory and adds that directory to your user PATH. ai-memory setup then does what it does on Linux and macOS, with a logon entry in place of the service: the server starts when you sign in, with no console window, and restarts if it fails. Details and the other Windows setups (WSL2, Docker Desktop, a real Windows service) are in docs/windows.md.

With Scoop (ai-memory 3.4.0 or later):

scoop bucket add akitaonrails https://github.com/akitaonrails/scoop-bucket
scoop install ai-memory
ai-memory setup

Update it with scoop update ai-memory.

Arch Linux (AUR)

For native Arch installs, use the AUR packages. They install /usr/bin/ai-memory, packaged hook sources, and both system-level and user-level systemd units.

yay -S ai-memory-bin    # prebuilt Linux x86_64/aarch64 binary
yay -S ai-memory        # builds from source
ai-memory setup         # data dir, user service, agents, self-check

Homebrew (macOS and Linux)

The tap installs the prebuilt binary and its hook sources on macOS and on Linux, including atomic distributions such as Bazzite or Fedora Silverblue where Homebrew is the usual way to add tools:

brew install akitaonrails/tap/ai-memory
ai-memory setup         # data dir, user service, agents, self-check

Use either ai-memory setup or brew services start ai-memory, not both. Details are in docs/install.md.

Fedora (RPM)

Download the x86_64 or aarch64 RPM from the latest release, then install it:

sudo dnf install ./ai-memory-*.rpm

On a single-user workstation, ai-memory setup then does the rest, as on the two-command path above: data dir and token, a user service, the agents it finds, and a self-check.

ai-memory setup

System service installs use /var/lib/ai-memory and /etc/ai-memory/ via the packaged unit. Full user-service, system-service, auth, and provider setup is in docs/install.md#arch-linux-native-packages-aur.

macOS (menu bar app)

A self-contained .app that bundles the native ai-memory binary and hooks/ tree, starts the existing LaunchAgent, and opens /web, ai-memory status, and config.toml from the menu bar. Wiki, SQLite, config, and models stay in ~/Library/Application Support/ai-memory, so replacing the app is an update and does not rewrite that tree.

Needs a Rust toolchain and Xcode / Swift 6 (same as a source build):

git clone https://github.com/akitaonrails/ai-memory
cd ai-memory
./companions/ai-memory-macos/build.sh
open "companions/ai-memory-macos/dist/AI Memory.app"

Drag AI Memory.app to /Applications, then Install & Start Server from the menu extra (no Dock icon). The app reads the bearer token init wrote into its data dir, so the status item turns green on its own. Then wire your agents with the bundled binary; --no-service leaves the app's LaunchAgent in charge:

BIN="/Applications/AI Memory.app/Contents/Resources/runtime/ai-memory"
"$BIN" setup --no-service

Prebuilt tarball and launchd-without-the-app paths: docs/macos.md. Companion details: companions/ai-memory-macos.

Docker

You need: Docker or Podman + an agent CLI from the Support Matrix, or anything else that speaks MCP.

The published Docker image includes linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 variants, so Apple Silicon Macs and ARM64 Linux hosts can pull akitaonrails/ai-memory without --platform linux/amd64 emulation.

The Docker quick-start below has no authentication: the container never runs init, so it starts without a token. The server binds to loopback only, so nothing outside the machine can reach it, but local processes and browser pages can. Native installs that run ai-memory init get a bearer token by default; see Security below for that and for adding a token here.

# 1. Install the ai-memory CLI wrapper (a small shell script that
#    runs the binary inside a container with your $HOME mounted). This is
#    the only thing that needs to live on the host filesystem.
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin
wrapper_tmp="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "$wrapper_tmp"' EXIT
wrapper_base=https://github.com/akitaonrails/ai-memory/releases/latest/download/ai-memory-wrapper
curl -fsSL "$wrapper_base" -o "$wrapper_tmp/ai-memory-wrapper"
curl -fsSL "$wrapper_base.sha256" -o "$wrapper_tmp/ai-memory-wrapper.sha256"
expected="$(awk 'NR == 1 { print $1 }' "$wrapper_tmp/ai-memory-wrapper.sha256")"
if command -v sha256sum >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    actual="$(sha256sum "$wrapper_tmp/ai-memory-wrapper" | awk '{ print $1 }')"
else
    actual="$(shasum -a 256 "$wrapper_tmp/ai-memory-wrapper" | awk '{ print $1 }')"
fi
[ -n "$expected" ] && [ "$actual" = "$expected" ] || { echo "wrapper checksum mismatch" >&2; exit 1; }
install -m 0755 "$wrapper_tmp/ai-memory-wrapper" ~/.local/bin/ai-memory
rm -rf "$wrapper_tmp"
trap - EXIT
# Most distros put ~/.local/bin on PATH automatically. If `which
# ai-memory` comes up empty, add this to ~/.bashrc / ~/.zshrc:
#     export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

# 2. Start the server. `--restart unless-stopped` makes it come back
#    on docker daemon restart and on machine boot (provided your
#    docker service is enabled at boot — `sudo systemctl enable
#    docker` on most distros). Loopback-only bind (`127.0.0.1:49374`)
#    so nothing outside this machine can reach it. Omit the LLM /
#    EMBEDDING lines for zero-LLM mode — FTS5 search still works
#    without any keys.
docker run -d --name ai-memory \
    --restart unless-stopped \
    -p 127.0.0.1:49374:49374 \
    -v ai-memory-data:/data \
    -e AI_MEMORY_LLM_PROVIDER=anthropic \
    -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... \
    -e AI_MEMORY_EMBEDDING_PROVIDER=openai \
    -e OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... \
    docker.io/akitaonrails/ai-memory:latest

# 3. Wire your agent CLI in two commands. The wrapper takes care of
#    mounts and each client's config-path detection. Re-run with
#    `--agent codex`, `--agent command-code`, `--agent devin`, `--agent opencode`, `--agent opencode2`, `--agent gemini-cli`,
#    `--agent grok`, `--agent kimi-code`, `--agent kiro-cli`, `--agent copilot-cli`, `--agent droid`, `--agent muse`, `--agent cline`, `--agent qwen-code`, `--agent qoder`, `--agent omp`,
#    `--agent oh-my-pi`, `--client cursor`,
#    `--client gemini-cli`, `--client grok`, `--client kiro-cli`,
#    `--client cline`, `--client freebuff`, etc.
#    for additional agents; full list in docs/install.md.
ai-memory install-mcp   --client claude-code --apply
ai-memory install-hooks --agent  claude-code --apply

On Linux and macOS, the Docker wrapper runs install-hooks through its checksum-verified native host client. Global options may precede the command, for example ai-memory --config /path/to/config.toml run codex; the native client receives the complete argument list. The installed hooks therefore enforce client-side capture controls such as [capture] ignore_paths and allowlist mode before an event reaches the spool or network. Set AI_MEMORY_HOOK_PLATFORM=posix explicitly only when you need the legacy shell compatibility path; the installer warns that path cannot enforce capture policy v1.

The examples use docker; replace it with podman on a Podman host. The wrapper automatically uses Podman when Docker is not installed. Set AI_MEMORY_DOCKER=podman to force Podman when both engines are available.

That completes the setup on Linux/macOS. Start a Claude Code session as usual: every prompt and tool call now lands in ai-memory, and the next session you open in this project will see a handoff with where you left off. On macOS the native binary is the recommended path when you do not need Docker, either through the menu bar app above or a release tarball / launchd agent. Later updates for that path use ai-memory upgrade (checksum-verified GitHub release replace + hook refresh); see docs/install.md#keeping-ai-memory-up-to-date. The same native upgrade path covers Windows x86_64 zip installs under a writable prefix (see docs/windows.md Scenario C). Upgrading a 2.x install of any kind to 3.0? Read docs/upgrading-to-3.0.md first.

Wiring another agent is the same two commands with a different name: --client codex, --agent codex, and so on for every row of the support matrix. OpenCode is version-detected by host-side commands; when generating its artifacts inside a container, use setup-agent --agent opencode --opencode-dialect v1|v2 --to /tmp/unused because the container cannot inspect the host executable. The legacy opencode2, opencode-v2, and open-code2 aliases remain force-V2 compatibility spellings for old scripts; use opencode for new commands. The full per-agent guide, including Windows and remote servers, is docs/install.md.

Two agents in the same project at once, or teammates on one server, work out of the box: the "current project" pointer is isolated per caller by default (v1.39+). See docs/auto-scope.md for the optional session-aware Claude Code bridge and the details.

If in doubt, start your harness with ai-memory run. It is the preferred way to launch: the first time it runs a harness it auto-installs that harness's ai-memory hooks + MCP if they are missing (so capture and recall work without a separate install-hooks/install-mcp step to forget), it wires the right project scope by construction, and it adds cross-harness session continuity on top of shared memory. Everything is idempotent and one-time per harness and config home. If the server is unreachable, run warns and launches anyway with local capture spooling; run ai-memory recover after the server returns (see Degraded offline launches). Pass --require-server to fail closed instead.

ai-memory run claude
ai-memory run codex --yolo   # same workstream + local Claude history dossier
ai-memory run --profile work claude  # reusable config.toml env/account preset
ai-memory continue           # resume the newest managed checkout
# after a dead launcher left its lease behind (same operator only)
ai-memory run --force-unlock codex
ai-memory resume             # pick from ALL workstreams in this checkout only
ai-memory resume --search auth # find a workstream by name (case-insensitive)
ai-memory resume --all       # pick across every linked checkout

--force-unlock immediately expires the selected workstream's active lease; use it only when you know the previous launcher is gone. It does not kill a native process, and it cannot evict another authenticated operator's run. See the managed-workstream recovery notes for the full safety contract.

On a real harness switch, the receiving managed agent is told to consult AI_MEMORY_PREVIOUS_SESSION_HISTORY when you ask to continue and the bounded portable packet lacks a detail. The variable names a private temporary Markdown projection created from the previous harness's checkout-validated, read-only adapter; the file disappears when the managed child exits. It is local to the launcher machine. This covers quota exhaustion and other abrupt exits where the old harness cannot write a handoff: refreshed ai-memory routing also tells the new agent that "continue", "resume", and "pick up where we left off" mean to read that file first when the three managed-run variables are present. A switch on another machine still gets the server's portable ledger and handoff, but cannot read a native transcript that exists only on the first machine.

Without the managed launcher, a harness cut off the same way leaves no handoff at all, so the next one could pick up an older handoff or session page. When the newest captured work in the project is in another of your sessions that never ended and left no handoff after that work, the next session start carries a one-line notice that names that session. The agent then reads its newest prompts and tool results with memory_read_session_observations. The same session is listed first in memory_briefing's recent_sessions, and memory_handoff_list names it as newer_unended_session.

If that variable is absent on a real same-machine switch, run type -a ai-memory and ai-memory --version in the launching shell. This path requires the 3.1.0 or newer host client; a stale Cargo or package-manager binary earlier in PATH can shadow an updated wrapper.

In resume, type to search, use Up/Down to select a workstream, and Left/Right to choose its harness. Enter launches the selection; Escape clears a search, then cancels when the search is empty (Ctrl-C always cancels). The list scrolls and loads every checkout-local page; there is no default workstream cutoff. Use --limit N only when you want to cap the matching results. Workstreams from other repositories or worktrees are left out unless you pass --all, which lists every linked checkout (the current one first); continue still resumes the newest linked checkout from anywhere. Listing reads Git identity only; it does not scan the working tree with git status before showing the picker. Full checkpoints are still captured when launching the selected workstream.

Auto-wiring is on by default; opt out with ai-memory run --no-autowire or AI_MEMORY_RUN_AUTOWIRE=false. You can still wire agents by hand with install-hooks / install-mcp (e.g. for a harness you never launch through ai-memory run).

ai-memory uninstall --apply removes everything ai-memory installed, and only what it installed. It also clears ai-memory run's auto-wire record, so the next managed launch wires that harness again; to keep it unwired, launch with --no-autowire or set AI_MEMORY_RUN_AUTOWIRE=false. Install commands are idempotent and write timestamped backups next to any file they touch.

NixOS

This flake ships a NixOS module (nixosModules.default) with a systemd.services.ai-memory unit: a dedicated ai-memory system user (nologin, no linger) plus a hardened systemd sandbox (ProtectSystem = "strict", empty capability sets, MemoryDenyWriteExecute, RestrictAddressFamilies, and the rest; see nix/systemd-sandbox.nix). Packaged FHS units under packaging/systemd/ keep their existing lighter hardening. The flake exports packages for x86_64-linux, aarch64-linux, and aarch64-darwin. Intel macOS remains supported by the release tarball and Homebrew, but not by the pinned Nixpkgs revision.

{
  inputs.ai-memory.url = "github:akitaonrails/ai-memory";

  outputs = { nixpkgs, ai-memory, ... }: {
    nixosConfigurations.myhost = nixpkgs.lib.nixosSystem {
      system = "x86_64-linux";
      modules = [
        ai-memory.nixosModules.default
        {
          services.ai-memory = {
            enable = true;
            # enableWeb = true;  # off by default — the web UI is opt-in
            # enableApi = true;  # API-only companions; no browser UI
            settings = {
              allowed_hosts = [ "localhost" "127.0.0.1" "::1" "homelab.example" ];
              log_level = "info";
            };
            # Loopback (default): secrets optional; missing env file is tolerated.
            # Non-loopback: set one of ageSecret, sopsSecret, or environmentFile.
            # ageSecret = "ai-memory-env";  # config.age.secrets.<name> (agenix)
            # sopsSecret = "ai-memory/env"; # config.sops.secrets.<name> (sops-nix)
          };
        }
      ];
    };
  };
}

Declarative non-secret config lives in services.ai-memory.settings (a small typed set for common keys, plus freeformType for the rest of config.toml). The module renders a generated TOML file and passes --config. Top-level bind, port, and enableWeb win over duplicate settings keys. Anything in settings (including llm_headers) lands in a world-readable Nix store path, so do not put API keys there.

Secrets such as AI_MEMORY_AUTH_TOKEN never go in settings or the world-readable Nix store. This includes llm_headers, which can carry API credentials; set AI_MEMORY_LLM_HEADERS in ageSecret, sopsSecret, or environmentFile instead. These three secret sources are mutually exclusive. Non-loopback binds require one; loopback may omit them and tolerates a missing environment file (systemd EnvironmentFile=-…). Put TLS in front of a LAN/WAN bind; see docs/https-via-proxy.md.

All options and defaults are in nix/nixos-module.nix. The module is entirely opt-in: nix build, nix run, nix develop, and the CLI are unchanged if you don't import it.

git is a runtime dependency. Hook capture and ai-memory doctor run it to read the repository a session works in. The module puts pkgs.git on the service's PATH. The package itself leaves the binary unwrapped, because a wrapper renames the running process and the live-process guard in reset, restore, reindex and uninstall --purge-data looks for a process named ai-memory. If you install the package without the module (nix profile install, home.packages), install git next to it.

Everyday use

Day to day, you mostly do not think about ai-memory. Hooks capture prompts, tool calls, and session boundaries; session end turns them into readable wiki pages; the next session starts with a handoff.

  • Ask "where did we leave off?" to continue from the pending handoff.
  • Import a local PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, Markdown file, or VTT/SRT transcript as attributed, sanitized memory with the optional ai-memory-importer document command.
  • Ask "have we discussed X?" or "search memory for Y" to query the wiki.
  • Narrow a large wiki before ranking with memory_query filters such as path_prefix: "procedures/", tag: "rust", kind: "decision", or tier: "procedural".
  • Inspect content-free per-workload LLM call, outcome, latency, and usage telemetry with ai-memory status --json; it diagnoses the configured provider but does not route different workloads to different models.
  • Ask "catch me up" for a prose digest of recent project activity, or run ai-memory recent (--global for every project) to list the newest pages.
  • Search Chinese, Japanese and Korean text without spaces: zero-LLM search matches unspaced Han, Kana and Hangul substrings.
  • Run ai-memory bootstrap once when adopting an existing project with months of history.
  • Start the server with --enable-web for a read-only browser view of the wiki, a link graph at /web/graph, a root/operator managed-workstream overview at /web/workstreams, and a JSON API under /api/v1. On a server with a bearer token and no user accounts (every fresh install), the browser asks for a username and password: any username, and the contents of <data_dir>/auth-tokens/default as the password.
  • Investigate Claude Code and Codex response-token usage in the project dashboard, and pick a Light, Dark or System theme. See Investigate token usage for capture coverage, cache accounting and the investigation flags. You can drill down from a project to an agent, its sessions and individual responses. The web agent inbox lets an operator queue requests for registered agents and read the received and sent history. Token filters run on the full authorized ledger, with native turn and tool context when reported. Pages show their sources, declared contradictions and recall explanations, and the feature guide shows the effective installation states in the web UI.
  • Back up host-side harness configuration with ai-memory backup-agents -o agent-assets.tar.gz; inspect a restore with ai-memory restore-agents -i agent-assets.tar.gz, then add --apply only after reviewing the active skills, plugins, instructions, and destinations.

Search modes, entities, feedback, briefings, and the web API are covered in docs/usage.md and docs/use-cases.md.

Teams and multiple machines

Run the server somewhere reachable, such as a homelab box or a LAN host, and point every machine and every teammate at it. Knowledge is shared per project; personal handoffs stay personal; every write is attributed and audited. Multi-user auth (passwords, API credentials) is built in.

Start with docs/users.md for accounts and ownership, and docs/deploy.md for the server itself. It includes measured capacity numbers and the one rule you must follow: one server per data directory, never two.

Two opt-in HTTP surfaces build on the same browser sign-in, and both are off by default. serve --enable-session-management lets signed-in users inspect sessions and purge the ones they own (docs/session-management.md). serve --enable-self-service-keys lets them issue and revoke their own aim_ API keys (docs/self-service-keys.md).

Security

The server binds to loopback only by default. A fresh ai-memory init also mints a root bearer token into the data dir, which the hooks, the CLI and the ai-memory mcp-bridge stdio bridge read from there; it is never written into a harness config. An install created before that default (and the Docker quick-start) runs without auth until ai-memory auth enable, and ai-memory status says so. From there, hardening is incremental: a bearer token for the LAN, per-user accounts, OIDC device auth for hooks, TLS via a reverse proxy. Capture is sanitized at a typed privacy boundary before anything is stored, and per-repository [capture] rules can exclude paths or invert to allowlist mode. A repository can also route its capture to a different server than the one the hooks were installed against. Human login beyond loopback requires an HTTPS posture by default. Operators who explicitly accept plaintext passwords, cookies, credentials, and memory traffic on a private LAN can opt in with serve --allow-insecure-human-auth; the server never enables that exception implicitly.

The full model is in docs/security.md, docs/users.md, and docs/https-via-proxy.md. For data-flow, identity/SSO, and offline-install questions specifically, see DATA_HANDLING.md, docs/sso.md, and docs/airgapped-install.md.

LLM providers

Optional. Everything works with zero LLM calls; adding a provider upgrades session summaries and enables semantic search. Anthropic, OpenAI (including OAuth), Codex CLI credential reuse, GitHub Copilot, Gemini, OpenCode (Go and Zen), the Cursor Agent CLI (cursor), and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM) are supported for consolidation; OpenAI, Voyage, Gemini, and keyless OpenAI-compatible endpoints for embeddings. Configuration lives in docs/llm-providers.md.

For optional synthesized query answers, operators can set [query_answer] max_context_tokens to limit admitted evidence while retaining all retrieval hits. Known newer corrections take priority, and whole snippets are preferred over sentence-bounded fragments. It is disabled by default. See the configuration reference for the conservative counting rule and omission receipt.

Architecture

One Rust binary runs an MCP/HTTP server and owns one data directory:

<data_dir>/
├── wiki/    # markdown source of truth, git-versioned
├── raw/     # immutable sanitized managed-workstream transcript segments
├── db/      # SQLite indexes, including FTS5, entities, and embeddings
├── models/  # reserved for local embedding models
└── logs/    # rolling tracing output

Hooks POST observations to the server. The server serializes writes through one SQLite writer, compiles session observations into markdown pages, and serves retrieval through FTS5, entity-match and graph-neighbor RRF, optional vector RRF, an observation-evidence stream that lifts a session's page when its captured turns match (on by default), bounded source-authority adjustment, and bounded raw-observation fallback for non-global searches.

See docs/ARCHITECTURE.md for the data-flow diagram, crate breakdown, schema notes, and invariants.

item.title: max-sixty/worktrunk
item.description:
Worktrunk is a CLI for Git worktree management, designed for parallel AI agent workflows

https://worktrunk.dev

  Worktrunk

November 2026: Worktrunk was released at the start of the year, and has quickly become the most popular git worktree manager. It's built with love (there's no slop!). Please let me know any frictions at all; I'm intensely focused on continuing to make Worktrunk excellent, and the biggest help is folks posting problems they perceive.

Worktrunk is a CLI for git worktree management, designed for running AI agents in parallel.

Worktrunk's three core commands make worktrees as easy as branches. Plus, Worktrunk has a bunch of quality-of-life features to simplify working with many parallel changes, including hooks to automate local workflows & copy-on-write build caches.

A quick demo:

📚 Full documentation at worktrunk.dev 📚

Context: git worktrees

AI agents like Claude Code and Codex can handle longer tasks without supervision, such that it's possible to manage 5-10+ in parallel. Git's native worktree feature gives each agent its own working directory, so they don't step on each other's changes.

But the git worktree UX is clunky. Even a task as small as starting a new worktree requires typing the branch name three times: git worktree add -b feat ../repo.feat, then cd ../repo.feat.

Worktrunk makes git worktrees as easy as branches

Worktrees are addressed by branch name; paths are computed from a configurable template. Commands that take a branch also accept the path of the worktree it is checked out in.

Start with the core commands

Core commands:

Task Worktrunk Plain git
Switch worktrees wt switch feat cd ../repo.feat
Create + start Claude wt switch -c -x claude feat 
git worktree add -b feat ../repo.feat && \
cd ../repo.feat && \
claude
Clean up wt remove 
cd ../repo && \
git worktree remove ../repo.feat && \
git branch -d feat
List with status wt list git worktree list (paths only)

Expand into the more advanced commands as needed

Workflow automation:

  • Hooks — run commands on create, pre-merge, post-merge, etc
  • LLM commit messages — generate commit messages from diffs
  • Merge workflow — squash, rebase, merge, clean up in one command
  • Interactive picker — browse worktrees with streaming CI status and diff, log, PR and comment previews
  • Share build caches — ten worktrees get target/, node_modules/, etc without building or copying them (on APFS, btrfs, and XFS)
  • wt list --full — CI status and AI-generated summaries per branch
  • PR checkout — wt switch pr:123 to jump straight to a PR's branch
  • Dev server per worktree — hash_port template filter gives each worktree a unique port
  • Aliases & per-branch variables — custom wt <name> commands and branch-scoped state for hook templates
  • ...and lots more

Multiple parallel agents, same simple commands:

Install

Homebrew (macOS & Linux):

brew install worktrunk && wt config shell install

Shell integration allows commands to change directories.

Cargo:

cargo install worktrunk && wt config shell install
Windows & other

Windows. wt defaults to Windows Terminal's command, so Winget additionally installs Worktrunk as git-wt to avoid the conflict:

winget install max-sixty.worktrunk
git-wt config shell install

Alternatively, disable Windows Terminal's alias (Settings → Apps → Advanced app settings → App execution aliases → "Terminal"/"Terminal Preview") to use wt directly.

Free code signing provided by SignPath.io, certificate by SignPath Foundation — policy.

Arch Linux:

sudo pacman -S worktrunk && wt config shell install

Conda / Pixi (community-maintained feedstock):

conda install -c conda-forge worktrunk && wt config shell install

Or with Pixi: pixi global install worktrunk && wt config shell install.

Quick start

Create a worktree for a new feature:

$ wt switch --create feature-auth
✓ Created branch feature-auth from main and worktree @ ~/repo.feature-auth

This creates a new branch and worktree, then switches to it. Do your work, then check all worktrees with wt list:

$ wt list
  Branch        Status       @±        ^↕        ^…±     Remote⇅  Commit    Age  Message
@ feature-auth  +   ↑      +27   -8   ↑1       +31                4bc72dc    2h  Add authenticatio…
^ main              ^⇡                                    ⇡1      0e631ad    1d  Initial commit

○ Showing 2 worktrees, 1 with changes, 1 ahead, hidden: Path

The @ marks the current worktree. + means staged changes, ↑1 means 1 commit ahead of main, ⇡ means unpushed commits.

When done, either:

PR workflow — commit, push, open a PR, merge via GitHub/GitLab, then clean up:

wt step commit                    # commit staged changes
gh pr create                      # or glab mr create
wt remove                         # after PR is merged

Local merge — squash, rebase onto main, fast-forward merge, clean up:

$ wt merge main
◎ Generating commit message and committing changes... (2 files, +53, no squashing needed)
  Add authentication module
✓ Committed changes @ a1b2c3d
◎ Merging 1 commit to main @ a1b2c3d (no rebase needed)
  * a1b2c3d Add authentication module
   auth.rs | 51 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
   lib.rs  |  2 ++
   2 files changed, 53 insertions(+)
✓ Merged to main (1 commit, 2 files, +53)
◎ Removing feature-auth worktree & branch in background (same commit as main, _)
○ Switched to worktree for main @ ~/repo

For parallel agents, create multiple worktrees and launch an agent in each:

wt switch -x claude -c feature-a -- 'Add user authentication'
wt switch -x claude -c feature-b -- 'Fix the pagination bug'
wt switch -x claude -c feature-c -- 'Write tests for the API'

The -x flag runs a command after switching; arguments after -- are passed to it. Configure post-start hooks to automate setup (install deps, start dev servers).

Next steps

  • Learn the core commands: wt switch, wt list, wt merge, wt remove
  • Set up hooks for automated setup
  • Explore LLM commit messages, interactive picker, Claude Code integration, CI status & PR links
  • Browse tips & patterns for recipes: aliases, dev servers, databases, agent handoffs, and more
  • Extending Worktrunk — customize workflows with hooks & aliases
  • Watch @DevOpsToolbox's video on Worktrunk
  • Run wt --help or wt <command> --help for quick CLI reference

Contributing

  • ⭐ Star the repo
  • Tell a friend about Worktrunk
  • Open an issue — feedback, feature requests, even a small friction or imperfect user message, or a worktree pain not yet solved
  • Share: X · Reddit · LinkedIn

📚 Full documentation at worktrunk.dev 📚
